summary:
Malawi criminalises consensual same-sex conduct. Penal Code sections 153, 154 and 156 remain in force, and the provisions reach gender identity directly through their application to people whose gender expression departs from expectations; Human Rights Watch reports that people whose gender expression differs from expectations are the most likely to be targeted. Under sections 153 and 156 men face up to fourteen years' imprisonment and women five years, and the sections were before the courts in 2024 as carrying up to fourteen years.

On 28 June 2024 a three-member panel of the Constitutional Court rejected the challenge to those sections. The application had been brought by Dutch national Jan Willen Akster and Jana Gonani, a trans woman who received an eight-year sentence in a men's prison in December 2021. Faith-based groups filed briefs and religious leaders led nationwide protests claiming the case sought to legalise same-sex marriage. The court left any reform to parliament. Human Rights Watch called the decision a dark day and warned that it exposes LGBT people to heightened risks of arbitrary arrest and violence.

Enforcement has been intermittent and evasive rather than absent. A justice-ministerial moratorium on arrests announced in 2012 was reaffirmed in December 2015, then suspended by the Mzuzu High Court in 2016 following litigation by religious leaders, leaving its legality contested. In April 2018 police in Mzuzu arrested Limbani Sibande, 24, for suspected homosexuality and charged him under section 156 rather than section 153, a choice that circumvented the six-year moratorium while both laws faced constitutional challenge; police spokespersons confirmed the custody.

Arbitrary detention and ill-treatment by police are documented. A 61-page Human Rights Watch report released on 26 October 2018, based on interviews with 45 LGBT people in Lilongwe and Blantyre alongside lawyers, activists and officials, found that police arbitrarily arrested and detained transgender people and at times assaulted them. Two men arrested on 7 December 2015 suffered house ransacking and assault by neighbours, threats of being burned alive, attempted extortion, forced stripping, forced medical and HIV and sexually transmitted infection examinations, and distribution of photographs on social media by community police.

Care access is compromised on gender-expression grounds. The same 2018 report records a trans man beaten and then refused treatment, and nurses mocking people presenting for HIV tests. Detention itself carries risk: Malawi's prisons were described as harsh in a 2011 United States State Department human rights report, and that report documented the July 2011 protest killings in which 20 people died.

Marriage and legal recognition are closed. The Marriage, Divorce and Family Relations Law, in force from 17 April 2015, bans all same-sex marriages and unions, states that gender is assigned at birth, and does not permit a person who has undergone gender reassignment surgery to marry someone of that person's prior gender. No process for legal gender recognition is described in the sources. There are no broad legal protections against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity; since 2019 the only limited protection is against hate speech, through sections 22(1-d) and 30(2-d) of the Communications (Broadcasting) Regulations 2019, which bar broadcast content likely to incite hatred on account of gender identity or sexual preference.

Official hostility is documented at the highest levels. In April 2010 President Bingu wa Mutharika called same-sex marriage evil and bad before the eyes of God, and in July 2011 he threatened activists Undule Mwakasungula and Gift Trapence, saying he would hunt them in their homes and smoke them out, forcing them into hiding amid treason threats. In January 2016 People's Party spokesperson Ken Msonda posted that gay people are worse than dogs and should be killed; the Malawi Law Society filed charges but the director of public prosecution took over the matter and discontinued it on 21 January. The Muslim Association of Malawi called for the death penalty for gay people in February 2014, and on 4 January 2017 thousands across 28 districts marched against legalising homosexuality in protests led by the Episcopal Conference of Malawi and the Evangelical Association of Malawi. Peter Sawali was arrested in 2010 and given a 60-day sentence for posting Gay rights are human rights posters in Blantyre.
tangentialFactors:
Community visibility exists but is fragile and provokes backlash. The country's first pride parade was held in Lilongwe on 26 June 2021, organised by the Nyasa Rainbow Alliance with more than 50 attendees who delivered a petition to city officials demanding marriage equality and better access to healthcare for LGBTQ people. Bail was denied to Tiwonge Chimbalanga and Monjeza in 2009 because the public was angry with them, and the magistrate said he sentenced them to protect society; international outlets failed to report Chimbalanga's gender identity during her trial. A January 2016 interview in which Eric Sambisa said kill us or give us our rights led to his brief police detention and time in hiding.

Malawi has resisted external pressure to decriminalise. At the 2011 Universal Periodic Review the government rejected every recommendation to decriminalise same-sex relations, stating that it had no plans to legalize homosexuality and should not be unduly singled out and unnecessarily pressured; recommendations had come from Sweden, Mexico, France, Canada, Germany, Australia, the United Kingdom, Italy, Austria, Ireland, Luxembourg, the United States, Spain, Switzerland and Norway. The UN Human Rights Committee's June 2012 provisional concluding observations urged Malawi to amend the Penal Code and protect same-sex couples from violence, and Malawi failed to file its ICCPR report for over 17 years. Donor pressure is contested domestically: the Malawi Council of Churches urged international organizations to refrain from using aid as a means of forcing the country to legalise sinful acts like homosexuality, and Justice Minister George Chaponda blamed civil society leaders for withdrawn foreign aid.

The government's own 2012 UN report stated that the vast majority of society has not accepted homosexuality and that homosexuality is not practiced in the open, and the country is described as highly conservative. Media and religious framing has been a recurring feature of the risk environment, including the 2011 claim that the constitutional case sought to legalise same-sex marriage and the March 2017 nationwide marches. State Department reporting in 2011 found senior officials created a discriminatory environment, citing tourism minister Daniel Liwimbi calling same-sex activity very un-Malawian. Against this, officials have at times argued for service access: in September 2009 Mary Shawa, secretary for nutrition, HIV and AIDS in the president's office, argued that Malawi must give gay people access to HIV and AIDS services on a human rights basis, and CEDEP's Gift Trapence contrasted the 2015 arrests with government Global Fund money for LGBTI HIV services.
localsOnly:
Residents live under a legal framework that assigns gender at birth and offers no procedure for legal gender recognition, so a person's documents continue to reflect the sex assigned at birth regardless of transition. The 2015 Marriage, Divorce and Family Relations Law bars same-sex unions and bars marriage between a person who has undergone gender reassignment surgery and someone of that person's prior gender, which constrains relationship recognition for trans residents as well as same-sex couples.

There is no general statutory protection against discrimination on sexual orientation or gender identity for residents; the only codified protection is the hate-speech limitation in the 2019 broadcasting regulations, which applies to broadcast content rather than to employment, housing, healthcare or education. Residents therefore depend on prosecutorial discretion, which has been inconsistent: a moratorium on arrests has existed on paper since 2012, was reaffirmed in December 2015, was suspended by the Mzuzu High Court in 2016, and was circumvented by at least one police charge in 2018.

Healthcare access on gender-expression grounds is documented as unreliable, including refusal of treatment after assault and mockery at HIV testing points, even as officials from 2009 onward have argued for inclusive HIV services and government Global Fund money funds LGBTI HIV programming. Community organisation operates openly in limited form: the Nyasa Rainbow Alliance has run public events since the June 2021 pride parade in Lilongwe, and domestic bodies including the Malawi Law Society, the Malawi Council of Churches and CEDEP have engaged with arrests, prosecutions and hate speech.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources do not state whether parliament took any action on Penal Code sections 153, 154 or 156 after the Constitutional Court's 28 June 2024 ruling, nor whether the government has announced a policy on enforcement since that date. Enforcement frequency after the ruling is unresolved in this inventory.

Whether the 2012 moratorium on arrests is legally operative remains unresolved: the Mzuzu High Court suspended it in 2016 following religious leaders' litigation, and no later judicial or executive determination is sourced here. The distinction in penalty between men and women under sections 153 and 156 is reported by Human Rights Watch, but the underlying statutory text is not reproduced in the inventory and the treatment of trans defendants under those provisions is not sourced.

No source in the inventory describes an administrative procedure, statutory or otherwise, for legal gender recognition in Malawi, and the absence of such a process is stated only descriptively in country coverage rather than confirmed against primary legislation. Several claims, including the 2015 marriage law provisions, the 2019 broadcasting regulation sections and the details of the December 2015 arrests, rest on secondary or encyclopedic sourcing that has not been checked against gazetted texts.

Whether the Communications (Broadcasting) Regulations 2019 hate-speech provisions have been invoked in any enforcement action is not documented in the inventory, nor is the current status of the prosecutions or charges described for Ken Msonda and Peter Sawali.
